introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2025. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde, puis les questions 1 à 12 réparties en quatre sections de trois questions) : filigranes gcerevision.com ignorés ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune citation ni statistique précise n'est avancée ; les dates, noms, traités et lieux sont ceux de l'historiographie établie, cités de mémoire historique et à faire relire par un historien avant mise en vente.

Question 3 : faits cités de mémoire historique (Lugard et le nord du Nigeria à partir de 1900, « warrant chiefs » de l'est du Nigeria, guerre des femmes d'Aba en 1929, quatre communes du Sénégal, loi de 1916 sur la citoyenneté, code de l'indigénat) ; aucune statistique précise n'est donnée, la faible proportion d'Africains devenus citoyens français est exprimée de façon qualitative.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Carefully examine the demerits of the colonial policies of Indirect Rule and Assimilation in West Africa.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Indirect Rule was the British method of governing colonies through existing African chiefs and institutions under the supervision of British officers. It was associated with Lord Lugard, who applied it in northern Nigeria from the early 1900s, and it was used in Nigeria, the Gold Coast, Gambia and Sierra Leone. Assimilation was the French policy of turning Africans into Frenchmen by teaching them the French language, culture and law, and giving the "assimilated" French citizenship; it was practised above all in Senegal (the four communes of Saint-Louis, Gorée, Rufisque and Dakar). Both policies were presented as practical and even generous, but both had serious demerits (faults and disadvantages) for the Africans, which are examined below.

**1. Demerits of Indirect Rule.**
- *It strengthened the power of chiefs and made them abusive.* Because the chiefs were backed by the British, they could rule without the control of their people. Many collected taxes unfairly, took bribes and used forced labour, and in the northern emirates the emirs kept their autocratic power.
- *It created artificial chiefs and conflicts.* In societies without chiefs, such as many Igbo communities of eastern Nigeria, the British appointed "warrant chiefs" who had no traditional authority. They were resented, and this contributed to the Aba women's riots of 1929 against the fear of taxation of women and the power of the warrant chiefs. The system had to be reformed after the protest.
- *It delayed modernisation and political progress.* The policy supported traditional rulers who were often illiterate and conservative, and it kept the educated Africans out of government, since the British distrusted the new elite as "agitators". In the north of Nigeria, Christian missions were largely kept out and western education developed slowly, so the region was far behind the south in schools and trained people at independence.
- *It encouraged regional and ethnic divisions.* By ruling each area through its own institutions, the system kept peoples apart and strengthened regionalism, for example the division between northern and southern Nigeria, which later troubled the country's politics.
- *It served British interests.* It was cheap, because few British officials were needed and Africans paid for the administration through taxes, and it allowed the colonial power to exploit the economy while chiefs took the blame for unpopular measures. It also made chiefs agents of the colonial power, which reduced their legitimacy in the eyes of their people.
- *It was not suited everywhere.* It worked best where there was a strong centralised system such as the emirates, but where there was none it was artificial or did not work, as in the Igbo area, and in the Gold Coast it was resented by the educated elite who wanted a share in government.

**2. Demerits of Assimilation.**
- *It despised African culture.* It treated African civilisation as inferior and tried to replace local languages, religion and customs with French ones, producing cultural alienation.
- *It reached very few Africans.* Only a small educated minority, mostly in the four communes, became French citizens, while the great majority remained "subjects" ruled by the harsh code of the indigénat, which allowed administrators to punish them without trial and to impose forced labour. The policy therefore promised equality but gave it only to a very few.
- *It was contradictory and costly.* France was not ready to give equal rights to millions of Africans, since that would have given them a large voice in Paris. Education was costly and limited, and the policy was replaced in practice, in the early twentieth century, by a policy of "association", which kept more African institutions.
- *It weakened African institutions and chiefs.* The French reduced the power of traditional chiefs and ruled directly through appointed chiefs and officials who obeyed Paris, which weakened African political systems.
- *It produced an uprooted elite.* The "évolués" often felt that they belonged neither to the French nor to the African world, and they were frequently disappointed by discrimination. Their frustration, however, also gave rise to demands for equal rights and later for independence.

**3. Comparison.** Both policies were a form of control for the benefit of the colonisers. Indirect Rule preserved African forms but emptied them of independent power; Assimilation destroyed African forms and offered an equality that was seldom delivered. Both exploited the economy and neglected the mass of the people.

**Conclusion.** The demerits of Indirect Rule and Assimilation were many: abuses, divisions, slow modernisation, cultural alienation and exploitation. Although each had some advantages, such as relatively cheap government and the training of an educated class, these did not outweigh the damage they caused, and they left problems that independent states had to face.
